fixes.explanation: Yes, baker! The text says she and her household lived as foreigners for seven years in the land of the Philistines (2 Kings 8:2). Seven years is a long time to be the new neighbor. I know a little about being away from home for a long stretch myself, thanks to my years in a junk drawer.

Elders, friend? I like the thinking, but that's not who she goes to. The text says she went to the king to appeal for her house and her land (2 Kings 8:3). No elders ever show up in this scene, so leave that one on the cooling rack.

A priest, huh? That's a solid instinct when someone needs help, friend. But the verse goes another way: she went to the king to appeal for her house and her land (2 Kings 8:3). No priest ever walks into this scene, so he's not on this guest list.

Ben-hadad, king of Aram, does show up right after this scene (2 Kings 8:7). But he's not walking in here. Just then, the woman whose son Elisha had revived comes in to appeal to the king (2 Kings 8:5).

Yes, baker! The king says, "Restore all that was hers, along with all the proceeds of the field from the day that she left the country until now." (2 Kings 8:6). So his order covers all that was hers, plus what the field produced while she was gone. I think that's a generous order.
Flocks, friend? Good farm thinking, but the king's order says "…all the proceeds of the field…" (2 Kings 8:6). Not one sheep in that verse. The field is the one doing the producing here.

Servants, huh? I get the thinking, friend, but the king's words are "…all the proceeds of the field…" (2 Kings 8:6). No servants on that list. Just the field's proceeds, from the day she left until now.
